title: Security, hosting and POPIA disclosure
subtitle: Okiru ESG Intelligence Platform — vendor due-diligence pack
meta: Prepared for Super Group IT  ·  Version 1.0  ·  16 September 2026
stamp: Okiru ESG Intelligence Platform · Security, hosting and POPIA disclosure · v1.0 · 16 September 2026 · Commercial in confidence
intro: This document describes how the Okiru ESG Intelligence Platform is hosted, how client data is encrypted, which artificial-intelligence services process it and where, how it is backed up, how access is controlled and logged, and how the platform sits against the Protection of Personal Information Act.

It is written for an IT function performing vendor due diligence, so it states what is not in place as plainly as what is. A reader who finds an unlisted weakness is entitled to assume there are others; the open items in section 9 are listed with an owner and a date so they can be assessed rather than discovered.

verification.label: Basis of this disclosure
verification.body: Every statement was read off the running production system on 16 September 2026 — the Azure resource configuration, the Kubernetes cluster, the deployed configuration key names, the backup store and the source repository. Nothing here is aspirational. Where a control is planned rather than live, it appears in section 9 and nowhere else.

sections.title: Where the platform runs, and where the data sits

blocks.text: The platform runs on Microsoft Azure in the South Africa North region (Johannesburg). All primary client data — the operational database, the cache, the document store and the backup store — is created and held in that region.

head: Component
Service
Region
Notes
rows: HTTPS enforced, TLS 1.2 minimum, public blob access disabled
Private registry, pull credentials held in-cluster

blocks.text: The platform is a multi-tenant application. Client records are separated logically by organisation, enforced in the application's authorisation layer, rather than by a separate database per client.

blocks.text: Encryption at rest is therefore present everywhere client data is stored, using Microsoft-managed keys. Customer-managed keys — where Super Group would hold and could revoke the key — are not configured today and are listed as an open item.

sections.title: Which models process client data, and where

blocks.text: The platform uses artificial intelligence in two places: reading uploaded documents (optical character recognition and layout extraction) and interpreting their contents against the ESG and B-BBEE data model. These run on different services, in different countries, and the distinction matters for data residency.

blocks.label: Cross-border processing — disclose and address
blocks.text: Document reading stays in South Africa. Interpretation does not: the Azure OpenAI resource is provisioned in East US on a Global Standard deployment, which permits Microsoft to process a request in any Azure region worldwide. Content sent for interpretation therefore leaves South Africa. This is a transfer of personal information outside the Republic under section 72 of POPIA and requires a lawful basis. Remediating it by moving to a South African or contractually region-pinned deployment is open item 1 in section 9.

items: Both services are Microsoft first-party Azure services consumed under the Azure enterprise agreement, not third-party AI vendors.
Microsoft does not use Azure OpenAI customer data to train its models, and prompts are not shared with other customers.
No open-weight, self-hosted or consumer AI service processes client data. A key for one third-party inference provider exists in configuration but is empty and no traffic is sent to it.
Extracted figures are always presented for human review before they are scored or published; the platform does not act on a model's output without a person seeing it.

sections.title: What is recorded when someone acts on client data

blocks.text: The platform writes a unified audit record for security-relevant actions across both application servers. Each entry carries the timestamp, the acting user, the organisation, the action, the resource type and identifier, whether it succeeded or failed, the source IP address, the user agent, the request identifier and the HTTP method and path.

head: Aspect
Position
Status
rows: Authentication, authorisation decisions, and record creation, change and export
Dedicated collection in the operational database, included in the nightly backup
Stored alongside application data; not written to append-only or immutable storage
No defined retention or archival period
No facility for a client to retrieve its own audit trail
Azure platform logs available; not centralised or retained to a defined policy

blocks.text: In POPIA terms Super Group is the responsible party for its own employee and operational data, and Okiru is an operator processing that data on its instruction. The following is our position condition by condition.

head: Condition
Position
Status
rows: Information Officer registration with the Information Regulator to be confirmed
Data processed only to produce the client's ESG and B-BBEE outputs; no secondary use, no resale, no profiling
Purpose set by the engagement; retention period not yet formally defined
No further processing beyond the stated purpose
Extracted values are shown for human correction before scoring; provenance recorded per figure
This document; a processing register per client is an open item
Encryption, access control and audit logging as set out above, with the gaps listed
Access and correction handled on request through the client; no self-service facility
Interpretation processing occurs outside South Africa — see section 3
Contactable breach process; no written, tested incident-response plan

blocks.label: Operator agreement
blocks.text: Section 21 of POPIA requires a written agreement between a responsible party and its operator obliging the operator to maintain the security safeguards in section 19. We recommend this disclosure be attached to such an agreement rather than standing alone, and we will sign one on Super Group's paper.

sections.title: How Super Group's systems would connect

items: Traffic is HTTPS only, TLS 1.2 or better, to a single named host with a publicly verifiable certificate.
Super Group would allow-list our egress addresses; we would allow-list theirs. Both are static.
Authentication for a system-to-system integration would be a per-client credential with least-privilege scope, rotatable on request and revocable immediately.
We accept data being pushed to us or exposed for us to pull. We do not require access to any Super Group system beyond the agreed endpoint and fields.
The field list Super Group's IT function would need to expose is issued separately as an interface specification, derived from the ESG data model rather than from any one company's spreadsheet.

sections.title: What is not in place, and when it will be

blocks.text: These are listed in the order we intend to close them. Items 1 to 4 we consider prerequisites to holding Super Group production data.

Move to a multi-node pool with an uptime SLA and run the database with redundancy
No rate limiting or web application firewall on public endpoints
Add request rate limiting to authentication endpoints and place a managed WAF in front of the ingress

Rehearse a full restore into an isolated environment and agree recovery point and time objectives in writing

Enforce for every account with access to client data
Password hashing work factor below current guidance
Raise the work factor and re-hash on next sign-in

Ship to append-only storage, set a retention period, and give clients a way to retrieve their own trail
No network segmentation between workloads in the cluster
Apply network policies so each component reaches only what it must
No automated build, test or dependency-vulnerability pipeline
Introduce continuous integration with tests and dependency scanning as a merge gate

Enable host encryption; offer customer-managed keys where a client requires them

Document, assign owners and test annually

Commission an external test and share the summary and remediation

sections.title: What we would put in place to protect Super Group's data

blocks.text: Asked what additional services would be needed, these are the ones we would add. They are listed with what each one actually buys, so the spend can be judged against the risk it removes rather than accepted as a list.

head: Service
What it protects against
Priority
rows: Azure Web Application Firewall (Front Door or Application Gateway)
Automated attacks, injection attempts and volumetric abuse reaching the application at all; also terminates TLS and absorbs denial-of-service traffic
Azure Key Vault with customer-managed keys
Key custody: Super Group could hold and revoke the key protecting its data at rest
Loss of the region, and the single-instance failure mode of a self-managed database
Microsoft Defender for Cloud (and for Containers)
Misconfiguration, vulnerable images and runtime threats going unnoticed
Azure Monitor / Log Analytics with retention
An incident that cannot be reconstructed afterwards because the logs had rotated away
Azure Private Link and private cluster endpoint
Exposure of management and data-plane endpoints to the public internet
Weaknesses we cannot see ourselves; also the evidence a client's auditor asks for
Azure OpenAI in a South African or pinned region
The transborder flow described in section 3
Dependency and secret scanning in the build pipeline
A vulnerable library or a committed credential reaching production
The financial consequence of a breach, which no control removes entirely
